raw_text:
### Introduction and Evolution
Sudden cardiac death (SCD) remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. While transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (TV-ICDs) are highly effective, their clinical utility is limited by lead-related complications, such as venous thrombosis, cardiac perforation, and systemic infection. To eliminate intravascular hardware, the subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed [1]. By positioning the entire system extrathoracically, the S-ICD leaves the heart and vascular system untouched [2]. Early validation studies [1] and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) investigational device exemption (IDE) trial [2] demonstrated high conversion efficacy for induced ventricular fibrillation (VF), which was subsequently corroborated by the post-market EFFORTLESS registry [3] and two-year pooled analyses [4].

### Landmark Comparative Trials and Long-Term Evidence
The landmark PRAETORIAN trial was the first randomized, head-to-head study comparing S-ICD and TV-ICD platforms, establishing S-ICD non-inferiority regarding device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [5]. In secondary analyses of the PRAETORIAN cohort, S-ICD patients had significantly lower rates of lead-related complications [6]. To optimize programming and minimize inappropriate therapies, the prospective UNTOUCHED trial enrolled primary prevention patients with low ejection fractions, reporting extremely low inappropriate shock rates using high-rate programming and discrimination filters [7]. 

Further randomized evidence came from the ATLAS trial, which demonstrated a 92% reduction in lead-related perioperative complications with the S-ICD compared to TV-ICDs [8]. In real-world cohorts, the 5-year S-ICD Post-Approval Study (PAS) confirmed robust long-term safety, reporting a procedural complication-free rate of over 93% and consistent shock efficacy over time [9]. Long-term registry data [10], matched cohort comparisons [11], and multi-center European outcomes [12] have repeatedly validated the durable efficacy of S-ICDs. While systemic infection is rare, pocket infections can occur, with risks thoroughly evaluated in the S-ICD PAS infection sub-analysis [13]. However, inappropriate shock rates, while declining with modern programming, remain a clinical consideration [14], as highlighted in recent meta-analyses [15].

### Surgical and Procedural Refinements
The surgical technique for S-ICD implantation has evolved rapidly. The original three-incision technique has largely been supplanted by the two-incision technique [16], which avoids a superior parasternal incision, reduces procedure times, and provides equivalent safety. Furthermore, transitioning the pulse generator from a subcutaneous pocket to an intermuscular or subserratus position [17] has reduced device protrusion, migration, and erosion. S-ICD procedures were historically performed under general anesthesia. However, ultrasound-guided regional anesthetic techniques—specifically the serratus anterior plane block and the transversus thoracic muscle plane block—have emerged as a safe approach [18], facilitating implantation under conscious sedation or monitored anesthesia care.

### Screening, Defibrillation Testing, and the PRAETORIAN Score
Because S-ICDs utilize far-field sensing, pre-implant electrocardiographic (ECG) screening is mandatory to verify that the patient has at least one suitable vector that avoids T-wave oversensing. To evaluate the implant position and predict conversion success without the need for VF induction, the PRAETORIAN score was developed based on post-implant chest radiographs [19]. This score-based approach served as the foundation for the randomized PRAETORIAN-DFT trial design [20], which established that omitting routine DFT during S-ICD implantation is safe and non-inferior [21]. Despite these structural validations, dynamic changes in ECG morphology can still impact vector eligibility, emphasizing the need for comprehensive screening protocols [22].

### Special Populations, Guidelines, and the Modular Future
The S-ICD is highly suited for patients with adult congenital heart disease [23], hypertrophic cardiomyopathy [24], and those with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) on hemodialysis [25] who are at high risk of central vein stenosis or device infection. Current international guidelines from the AHA/ACC/HRS [26] and ESC [27, 28] recommend the S-ICD with Class I or IIa indications for individuals without pacing requirements. Although S-ICDs cannot deliver chronic bradycardia pacing or anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP) [29], the modular cardiac rhythm management (mCRM) system has overcome this limitation. The MODULAR ATP trial proved that co-implanting a leadless pacemaker that communicates wirelessly with an S-ICD via conductive communication can safely and effectively provide both bradycardia pacing and ATP [30].
